reason: The sources thoroughly corroborate over a dozen specific facts detailing Giotto's dramatic flyby, impacts, and legacy across multiple independent sites.
story: In March 1986, Europe took a breathtaking gamble: hurling the Giotto probe straight toward the roaring heart of Halley's Comet at 150,000 miles per hour. Guided by Soviet pathfinder probes, the spacecraft dove within 370 miles of the nucleus, shielded only by a dual-layered Whipple bumper of thin aluminum and Kevlar. Just seconds before closest approach, a cometary dust grain slammed into Giotto, knocking the spacecraft into a violent spin and severing communications with Earth. As monitor screens at mission control in Darmstadt went blank, scientists feared the probe was destroyed. Yet, against all odds, Giotto's thrusters stabilized its orientation 32 minutes later, fully restoring the signal. Though its camera was ultimately shattered by another impact, Giotto captured humanity's first close-up images of a cometary nucleus, revealing a dark, peanut-shaped world violently venting jets of gas into deep space.
angle: Barreling into Halley's Comet at 150,000 miles per hour, Giotto took a direct dust hit seconds before closest approach that knocked out its Earth antenna and destroyed its camera—yet it survived to send humanity's first close-up images of a comet's core.

claims.claim: Giotto was launched on 2 July 1985 aboard an Ariane 1 rocket from Kourou, French Guiana.
Giotto was the European Space Agency's first deep-space mission.
The spacecraft was named after Italian Renaissance painter Giotto di Bondone, who observed Halley's Comet in 1301 and painted it into the Adoration of the Magi.
Giotto was designed and built by British Aerospace using a structure based on GEOS Earth satellites.
The spacecraft was protected by a Whipple shield made of a 1 mm aluminum front sheet and a 12 mm Kevlar rear sheet.
Soviet Vega spacecraft acted as pathfinders, tracking the comet's nucleus to help Giotto target its trajectory.
Giotto closed in on Halley's Comet at a relative speed of 68 kilometers per second (approximately 245,000 km/h).
Giotto made its closest approach to Halley's Comet on 13–14 March 1986 at a distance of 596 kilometers.
Seconds before closest approach, Giotto was struck by a cometary dust particle that knocked it off its spin axis.
The dust impact caused Giotto to lose communication with Earth because its high-gain antenna tilted out of alignment.
Giotto stabilized itself and fully restored radio communications with Earth after 32 minutes.
Giotto's Halley Multicolour Camera was permanently disabled by a dust impact during the encounter.
Giotto transmitted the first close-up photographs of a cometary nucleus, showing an irregular peanut- or potato-shaped body.
Images and data revealed that the comet's nucleus was extremely dark, with active outgassing jets venting material from the sunlit side.
On 2 July 1990, Giotto became the first interplanetary spacecraft to use Earth for a gravity-assist swing-by.
Giotto conducted a second comet flyby on 10 July 1992, passing within roughly 200 kilometers of Comet Grigg–Skjellerup.
Giotto spacecraft operations were officially terminated on 23 July 1992.

disputed: Timing of the wobble-inducing impact: Sources S1 and S3 state 7.6 seconds before closest approach, S2 states 15 seconds, and early news report S5 states 2 seconds before closest approach. Scripts should generalize to 'seconds before closest approach.'

Duration of signal loss: S1 and S3 report 32 minutes until full stabilization and contact restoration, whereas UPI report S5 states contact was lost for 25 minutes. Scripts should state 'roughly half an hour' or attribute 32 minutes to ESA records.
First Earth flyby altitude on 2 July 1990: S3 states 22,730 km while S6 states 16,300 km. Scripts should avoid mentioning the exact altitude or state 'between 16,000 and 23,000 kilometers.'
